It also shipped GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It , a Chrome extension for the same data. The site reads on-demand and spot prices from each provider’s own pricing page. The goal is simple: answer “what GPU do I need, and where is it cheapest?” in one place. What is GPU Leaderboard? GPU Leaderboard is a pricing dashboard that ranks rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. It is built for teams running inference. The v1 application has 4 views: Inference pricing: a cost calculator for a full run, not a single hourly rate. Leaderboard : every offer ranked by $/GPU-hr, filterable by GPU, tier, region and availability. Cheapest Inference : the lowest on-demand floor for each tracked GPU. Providers : a directory with instance counts, regions, status-page incidents and price-check history. How does the GPU inference cost calculator work? You pick an accelerator, GPU count, duration and utilization. The calculator then prices that exact run at every provider. An optional model field narrows the list. The default example is 8×H100 for 72 hours at 90% utilization. That bills 576 GPU-hours. The cheapest result is $967.68 at Latitude, at $1.68 per GPU-hour. The median across 15 providers is $1,716.48. The most expensive is $3,545.28 at CoreWeave. The calculator also shows a “real” cost per used GPU-hour. Idle time is still billed, so $1.68 at 90% utilization becomes $1.87. This is the number most budget sheets miss. What does the Deploy It Chrome extension do? GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It brings the price data to where developers pick models. Per its store listing, it works in 3 places: Hugging Face model pages: detects model size and estimates VRAM at FP16, INT8 and INT4. It then shows the cheapest hourly GPUs that fit. GitHub repos: detects model references and gives a hardware estimate in place. Toolbar lookup: search any model or GPU from the browser toolbar. Key Takeaways GPU Leaderboard ranks 201 live GPU offers from 24 providers by $/GPU-hr. Its calculator prices a full run, including idle time at your utilization. Deploy It shows VRAM needs and cheapest GPUs on Hugging Face and GitHub. An 8×H100, 72-hour run spans $967.68 to $3,545.28 across multiple providers. Coverage and daily refresh are the main gaps versus older trackers. Try it at gpuleaderboard.com and install the Deploy It extension from the Chrome Web Store. The post MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. It returns calibrated probabilities for up to 1,000 yes/no, choice and rubric questions over text, images, audio, video and PDFs, at $0.10 per 1M input tokens. The post Google Launches Gemini Decisions API With Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10/M Tokens appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API , powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 ( gemini-decision-1 ). The Gemini Decisions API does not generate text. It scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities. For developers, this targets the small branching calls inside agents: routing, policy checks, tool selection and grading. Google prices it at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with zero output tokens billed. TL;DR Size: Context is 262,144 tokens (256K) across shared input and all questions. Runs on: Google-hosted API only (Gemini Developer API, v1beta). No open weights or self-hosting. Performance: Leads 7 of 9 accuracy benchmarks in Google’s table, with the lowest calibration error. Best: 92.2% on JevBench (public split). Worst: 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI, its lowest score. It also trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call (79.9% vs 82.0%). Bottom line: Best: multimodal, calibrated decisions in 150-250 ms. Worst: not the cheapest; Jev 1.14 costs $0.68 vs $0.88 on the shared suite. What is the Gemini Decisions API? Gemini Decision 1 is a specialized multimodal model from Google built for closed-set decisions. It reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in one prefill pass. Output token usage is always 0. Your code branches directly on the returned numbers. Each request has 3 parts: a model ID, a shared input , and a map of questions. The docs define 3 question types: noul (yes/no): returns the probability of yes, bounded between 0.01 and 0.99. choice : picks 1 of 2 to 255 options and returns normalized probabilities for every option. score : rates input on 2 to 255 ordered rubric levels and returns a probability-weighted score. Every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1. Google suggests routing low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer. Questions are scored in parallel and cannot see each other. How does Gemini Decision 1 work? Standard models decode an answer token by token, then your code parses it. Gemini Decision 1 instead scores your candidate options in one forward pass. Google reports median model compute of 50-100 ms and 150-250 ms end to end. That holds for inputs up to 16K tokens and stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions. Billing follows the same design. The shared input is billed once per request, however many questions you ask. Each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens. There are no thinking-token, transcription or OCR charges. Gemini Decision 1 benchmarks Google tested Gemini Decision 1 against 3 rivals. They are TypeSafe Jev 1.14 , GPT-6 Luna on OpenAI Decisions and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. All figures below are self-reported by Google. Refusals and safety blocks count as incorrect. Benchmark Gemini Decision 1 TypeSafe Jev 1.14 GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI Decisions) Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite JevBench (public split) 92.2% 90.0% 90.9% 86.6% Amazon ESCI (Macro-F1) 58.7% 56.7% 54.7% 47.2% New Yorker Caption (text-only) 79.7% 72.0% 68.4% 73.7% Mind2Web Multimodal 86.2% 86.8% 81.8% 78.0% PubMedQA 79.8% 78.2% 74.4% 77.6% Global-MMLU-Lite (non-English) 86.0% 85.0% 79.6% 78.8% When2Call 79.9% 82.0% 70.4% 60.9% MMAU (audio) 71.8% Not reported Not reported 67.7% Video-MME (no subtitles) 69.1% Not reported Not reported 63.3% Top-1 ECE (lower is better) 0.0250 0.0494 0.0721 0.2104 Total price, 7 shared evals $0.88 $0.68 $0.93 $4.14 Source: Google blog benchmark table . The calibration result is the clearest gap. Gemini Decision 1’s error of 0.0250 is about half of Jev 1.14’s 0.0494. That matters when you set confidence thresholds for automation. On cost, Google says it is nearly 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite across the shared suite ($0.88 vs $4.14).
